s: 22 million specimens under one Oakland roof
w: Twenty-two million specimens live behind these Oakland walls, stacked up since steel money built the place in 1896. Andrew Carnegie wanted Pittsburgh to have a natural history collection to rival anywhere - the paleontology and entomology wings still do the heavy lifting.
_facts: founded by Andrew Carnegie in 1896
Oakland neighborhood of Pittsburgh
houses about 22 million specimens
extensive paleontological and entomological collections

s: Where two rivers made a third, and a fort
w: British troops raised this fort in 1759 at the exact point where the Monongahela and Allegheny meet to form the Ohio - ground the French had just abandoned, torching Fort Duquesne rather than surrender it. The site that grew into Pittsburgh started right here.
_facts: built by British forces 1759-1761 during the French and Indian War
sits at the confluence forming the Ohio River
near the site of Fort Duquesne, destroyed by the French in 1758
led to the development of Pittsburgh

s: Seven floors, one Pittsburgh-born pop icon
w: The largest museum in North America devoted to a single artist sits on the North Shore, seven floors deep in the hometown boy's own obsessions - 900 paintings, thousands of photographs, over 4,000 films and videotapes. Warhol left Pittsburgh; Pittsburgh built him a shrine anyway.
_facts: largest museum in North America dedicated to a single artist
North Shore of Pittsburgh
900 paintings, ~2,000 works on paper, over 1,000 prints, 77 sculptures, 4,000 photographs, 4,350+ films/videotapes
collaborative project of Carnegie Institute, Dia Art Foundation and the Andy Warhol Foundation

s: The gallery that outgrew its name three times
w: Opened for viewing in 1895 as the plain old 'Department of Fine Arts,' this Oakland gallery kept tripling in size and changing its name to match - Museum of Art in 1963, Carnegie Museum of Art in 1986. One of Andrew Carnegie's four museums, still growing into the title.
_facts: originally the Department of Fine Arts, Carnegie Institute
first gallery opened for public viewing on November 5, 1895
new building on Forbes Avenue built 1907
renamed Museum of Art, Carnegie Institute in 1963, then Carnegie Museum of Art in 1986

s: A step-pyramid crown, and a bomb on floor 29
w: Gulf Oil's 1932 headquarters wears a step-pyramid crown modeled on the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, a mausoleum for an oil company. In 1974 the Weather Underground detonated a bomb on the 29th floor, protesting Gulf's stake in Angola's oil fields. It survived that, and a 2021 fire too.
_facts: 44-story Art Deco skyscraper completed 1932 for Gulf Oil Corporation
crown modeled after the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus
bomb detonated on the 29th floor June 13, 1974 by the Weather Underground protesting Gulf Oil's involvement in Angola
condemned after a fire in 2021, reopened after repairs

w: Steel money built this too: Henry Phipps gave Pittsburgh a fourteen-room Victorian glasshouse in 1893, still full of palms, bonsai and orchids under Lord & Burnham ironwork. Its newer production greenhouse was the first in the world to earn LEED Platinum - old glass, new conscience.
_facts: founded 1893 by Henry Phipps Jr. as a gift to Pittsburgh
set in Schenley Park
fourteen-room Victorian Lord & Burnham conservatory
production greenhouse was the first and only one to receive LEED Platinum certification

s: The mill where the Homestead Strike turned bloody
w: Andrew Carnegie bought this Monongahela riverside mill in 1883 and expanded it fast enough to feed an empire. In 1892 it became the stage for the Homestead Strike, one of the most notable labor disputes in American history - a confrontation the whole country watched.
_facts: steel mill on the Monongahela River at Homestead, Pennsylvania
purchased by Andrew Carnegie in 1883 and rapidly expanded
supplied by the Union Railroad and lake steamships
site of the Homestead strike of 1892, one of the most notable labor disputes in US history

s: Carnegie's science wing, across from the Steelers
w: One of Andrew Carnegie's four museum siblings, this one traded oil paintings for hands-on science, planted in the Chateau neighborhood right across the street from Acrisure Stadium. Recently renamed from Carnegie Science Center, it is still the family's most hands-on member.
_facts: formerly known as Carnegie Science Center
one of the four Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh
located in the Chateau neighborhood, across from Acrisure Stadium

s: Pittsburgh's mother church, rebuilt twice over
w: St Paul Parish opened in Pittsburgh in 1833 and became a cathedral in 1843 - then burned down in 1851. The second cathedral went up in 1855; the third, consecrated in 1906, still stands and seats 3,000 worshippers. Third time was the charm for the Diocese's mother church.
_facts: St Paul Parish established 1833, became the Diocese of Pittsburgh's cathedral in 1843
first cathedral destroyed by fire in 1851, replaced 1855
third and current cathedral consecrated 1906
seats approximately 3,000 worshippers

s: Built to overshadow Andrew Carnegie, literally
w: Henry Clay Frick and Andrew Carnegie split as bitter business rivals, so Frick built his 1902 tower right next to Carnegie's - deliberately taller, deliberately overshadowing it. Daniel Burnham designed the 330-foot spite tower; its top floor still keeps the Union Club's handcrafted ceiling and brass fixtures.
_facts: built 1902 by Henry Clay Frick, designed by Daniel H. Burnham
at 330 feet was Pittsburgh's tallest building when it opened
built next to Andrew Carnegie's building, deliberately designed to overshadow it after their feud
top floor reserved for the Union Club of Pittsburgh, with handcrafted ceiling and brass fixtures

s: A WWII sub, docked in landlocked Pittsburgh
w: A Tench-class submarine built for World War Two now sits landlocked in Pittsburgh, the only US Navy ship ever named for the requin - French for shark. She has been a museum ship at the Science Center since 1990, hull intact, decades from open water.
_facts: Tench-class submarine
only US Navy ship named after the requin (French for shark)
museum ship since 1990 at the Science Center in Pittsburgh

s: 19,750 panes of glass, one skyline icon
w: Philip Johnson wrapped downtown Pittsburgh's newest skyscraper complex in 19,750 panes of matching glass, six buildings across three city blocks anchored by a 40-story tower. Built for PPG Industries and finished in 1984 at a cost of $200 million, the spires still anchor the skyline PPG's name once dominated outright.
_facts: complex of six buildings across three city blocks and 5.5 acres
designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee
all-glass design of 19,750 pieces of glass, anchored by the 40-story One PPG Place
built for PPG Industries, opened 1983-84, cost $200 million
